# Foundation Models for Segmentation {#sec-segmentation}

This chapter continues the segmentation story from @sec-detection-and-segmentation
and @sec-detr: from the classical formulation of **segmentation** as a dense,
per-pixel labelling problem, to the **Segment Anything** (SAM) family of
*promptable foundation models* developed by Meta AI. We first fix the
taxonomy of segmentation tasks (@sec-seg-tasks), then look at **instance
segmentation via detection** and the **Feature Pyramid Network** it relies on
(@sec-instance-seg) — the architectural ingredient, together with the
**DETR** transformer detector (@sec-detr), that SAM inherits. We then devote
the second half of the chapter to the SAM line itself — the original **SAM**
(@sec-sam), its video extension **SAM 2** (@sec-sam2), and the
open-vocabulary **SAM 3** (@sec-sam3).

## Segmentation Tasks {#sec-seg-tasks}

Segmentation asks a model to reason about an image *below* the level of
a single label or box. Three variants are worth distinguishing:

- **Semantic Segmentation** classifies **every pixel** of an image into a
  fixed set of categories. It does *not* separate two objects of the same
  class — all "cat" pixels receive the same label regardless of how many
  cats are present.
- **Instance Segmentation** additionally **distinguishes between distinct
  objects** of the same class, producing one mask per object instance.
- **Panoptic Segmentation** unifies the two by labelling **both countable
  "things"** (people, cars — which get instance identities) **and
  uncountable "stuff"** (sky, grass, road — which do not) at the pixel
  level.

![The spectrum of recognition tasks. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel but merges instances ("no objects, just pixels"); classification+localization handles a single object; object detection places boxes around multiple objects; instance segmentation produces a separate mask per object. *Source: Stanford CS231n / public-domain example image.*](/images/segmentation/segmentation_tasks.png){#fig-seg-tasks width=95%}

### Semantic segmentation architectures

- **U-Net (2015)** [@ronneberger2015unet] is the canonical semantic
  segmentation model: a convolutional **downsampling** (encoder) path that
  compresses the image into semantically rich, low-resolution feature
  maps, followed by a transposed-convolution **upsampling** (decoder) path
  that recovers full resolution. Crucially, **skip connections** copy
  feature maps from the encoder to the matching decoder stage, letting the
  network combine high-level semantics (what) with low-level spatial
  detail (where) for a sharp segmentation map.

![U-Net's symmetric encoder–decoder ("U") shape. The contracting path (Conv+BN+ReLU with pooling) reduces spatial resolution while increasing semantic depth; the expanding path (upsampling) restores resolution; skip-connections bridge matching resolutions so fine detail is preserved.](/images/segmentation/unet.png){#fig-unet width=60%}

- **DeepLab (2015)** takes an alternative view of the downsampling
  problem. Rather than pooling away spatial resolution, it introduces
  **dilated (atrous) convolutions**, which enlarge the receptive field
  *without* reducing resolution or adding parameters, and refines the
  coarse network output with a **fully-connected Conditional Random Field
  (CRF)** to sharpen object boundaries.

### Optimization: pixel-wise loss and class imbalance

The standard training objective for semantic segmentation is a
**pixel-wise softmax cross-entropy**, summed over classes at every pixel:

$$
\mathrm{CE} = -\sum_{\text{classes}} y_{\text{true}}\,\log\big(y_{\text{pred}}\big).
$$

Dense prediction, however, is dominated by *easy* background pixels, and
foreground/background class imbalance can swamp the gradient. **Focal
Loss** [@lin2017focal] addresses this by down-weighting well-classified
examples with a modulating factor $(1-p_t)^{\gamma}$:

$$
\mathrm{CE}(p_t) = -\log(p_t),
\qquad
\mathrm{FL}(p_t) = -\,(1-p_t)^{\gamma}\,\log(p_t),
$$

where $p_t$ is the model's estimated probability of the ground-truth
class and $\gamma \ge 0$ is a focusing parameter. As $\gamma$ grows, the
loss (and hence the gradient) contributed by confidently classified
pixels shrinks toward zero, concentrating learning on the **hard,
mis-classified** examples.

![Focal loss for several values of the focusing parameter $\gamma$. Setting $\gamma = 0$ recovers ordinary cross-entropy. Larger $\gamma$ suppresses the loss on well-classified ("easy") examples on the right, so the effective gradient is dominated by hard examples on the left. *Source: Lin et al., "Focal Loss for Dense Object Detection" (2017).*](/images/segmentation/focal_loss.png){#fig-focal width=70%}

## Instance Segmentation via Detection {#sec-instance-seg}

A productive family of instance-segmentation models is obtained by taking
a strong **object detector** and bolting on a **segmentation head** —
**Mask R-CNN** [@he2017maskrcnn] (already covered in detail in
@sec-maskrcnn) is the most influential example. Mask R-CNN is almost
always paired with a **Feature Pyramid Network (FPN)** [@lin2017fpn],
which is the piece we focus on here.

### Feature Pyramid Networks

The **Feature Pyramid Network** is the component that lets the region
proposal stage see objects across a wide range of sizes. A naive detector
predicts from a **single** high-level feature map, which is semantically
strong but spatially coarse — poor for small objects and for the fine
detail segmentation needs.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Single-feature-map prediction: only the deepest, coarsest map is used.](/images/segmentation/fpn_single_feature_map.png){#fig-fpn-single width=70%}

![Feature Pyramid Network: predictions are made at *every* level of a top-down pyramid, each level fusing coarse semantics with finer resolution.](/images/segmentation/fpn_schematic.png){#fig-fpn-schematic width=95%}
:::

Concretely, the FPN augments the bottom-up backbone (ResNet stages
$C_2,\dots,C_5$) with a **top-down pathway** and **lateral connections**.
Each top-down map $M_\ell$ is formed by upsampling the coarser map above
it (by $2\times$) and adding a $1{\times}1$-projected lateral feature from
the matching bottom-up stage; a $3{\times}3$ convolution then produces the
output pyramid level $P_\ell$. A shared predictor head (objectness +
bounding box) is applied to every level.

![FPN construction. The bottom-up ResNet path ($C_2$–$C_5$, strides 4–32) is mirrored by a top-down path ($M_5\to M_2$) with $1{\times}1$ lateral connections and $2\times$ upsampling; $3{\times}3$ convolutions yield the pyramid $P_2$–$P_5$. A lightweight predictor head (objectness + box) is shared across levels. *Source: FPN / Faster R-CNN literature.*](/images/segmentation/fpn_architecture.png){#fig-fpn-arch width=75%}

Given the pyramid, the RoI's feature patch is extracted from **the level
whose scale best matches the RoI's size**. For a region of interest of
width $w$ and height $h$, the pyramid level $k$ is chosen as

$$
k = \Big\lfloor\, k_0 + \log_2\!\big(\sqrt{wh}\,/\,224\big)\Big\rfloor,
\qquad k_0 = 4,
$$

so that larger RoIs are read off coarser (higher-$k$) maps and smaller
RoIs off finer maps; here $k$ indexes the $P_k$ layer of the FPN used to
generate the feature patch, and $224$ is the canonical ImageNet
pre-training size.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![Faster R-CNN with a single-scale feature map: region proposals and RoI features are drawn from one backbone output.](/images/segmentation/faster_rcnn_single_scale.jpg){#fig-frcnn-single}

![Faster R-CNN with an FPN backbone: proposals and RoI features are drawn from a multi-scale pyramid, improving small-object recall.](/images/segmentation/faster_rcnn_fpn.jpg){#fig-frcnn-fpn}
:::

Detection and segmentation were later unified under a single
**transformer** architecture — the **DETR** detection transformer and its
panoptic-segmentation extension, covered in @sec-detr — which removes
anchors and non-maximum suppression entirely by framing detection as
direct set prediction.

## SAM (Segment Anything Model): A Foundation Model for Segmentation {#sec-sam}

The original **Segment Anything (SAM, 2023)** [@kirillov2023sam] model —
its promptable-segmentation pre-training task, ViT image encoder, prompt
encoder, mask decoder, the SA-1B data engine, and its zero-shot transfer
properties — is covered in @sec-sam of the Vision Transformers chapter.
The rest of this chapter picks up where that section leaves off: SAM's
extension to video (**SAM 2**) and to open-vocabulary concept prompts
(**SAM 3**).

## SAM 2: Segment Anything in Images and Videos {#sec-sam2}

**SAM 2 (2024)** [@ravi2024sam2] generalizes SAM from static images to
**video**, unifying image and video segmentation under a single
**Promptable Visual Segmentation (PVS)** task. In PVS, a prompt (points,
box, or mask) may be supplied on **any frame**, and the model must produce
a **spatio-temporal mask** — a *masklet* — that segments and **tracks** the
target object through the entire clip, while remaining interactively
correctable: an extra click on a later frame refines the whole masklet.

![SAM 2 at a glance. **(a) Task:** promptable visual segmentation — a prompt (box, points, or mask) given on one or more frames yields object segmentation throughout the video. **(b) Model:** a per-frame image encoder feeds memory attention (conditioned on a memory bank) and a prompt-conditioned mask decoder, producing a valid mask on every frame. **(c) Data:** a model-in-the-loop data engine builds the SA-V dataset. *Source: Ravi et al., "SAM 2" (2024).*](/images/segmentation/sam2_task_model_data.png){#fig-sam2-overview width=95%}

![SAM 2 tracking a segmented object across frames in a video. *Source: Meta AI SAM 2 demo.*](/images/segmentation/sam2_demo.gif){#fig-sam2-demo width=85%}

The core challenge relative to images is **temporal consistency under
occlusion, appearance change, and re-identification**. SAM 2 addresses
this with a **streaming memory** architecture that processes frames one at
a time and conditions each prediction on what it has already seen:

- **Image encoder (streaming).** A **hierarchical (Hiera)** vision
  transformer encodes each incoming frame *once*, in a streaming fashion,
  producing per-frame embeddings — the video analogue of SAM's single-pass
  image encoder, enabling **real-time** interaction.
- **Memory bank.** A FIFO queue stores features and predicted masks from a
  window of **recent frames** plus the **prompted frames**, together with
  **object pointers** — compact tokens summarizing the object's appearance.
- **Memory attention.** Before decoding the current frame, transformer
  blocks let the frame embedding **cross-attend to the memory bank**, so
  the mask prediction is conditioned on the object's past appearance and
  motion.
- **Prompt encoder & mask decoder.** Essentially inherited from SAM, but
  now conditioned on the memory-attended features. As in SAM, **ambiguity
  is resolved by emitting multiple candidate masks** and keeping the
  highest-confidence one; an added **occlusion head** predicts whether the
  object is **present at all** in the current frame, which is essential for
  objects that leave and re-enter the view.

![SAM 2 streaming architecture. Each frame is embedded once by the **image encoder**; **memory attention** conditions the current embedding on features, past predictions, and object pointers stored in the **memory bank**; the **mask decoder** (fused with the **prompt encoder**) emits the mask, which the **memory encoder** writes back to the memory bank for future frames. Processing frames left-to-right in time makes segmentation streaming and real-time. *Source: Ravi et al., "SAM 2" (2024).*](/images/segmentation/sam2_model_architecture.png){#fig-sam2-arch width=95%}

Because a single image is just a one-frame video, this architecture
subsumes SAM: on still images SAM 2 is **more accurate and roughly
6× faster** than the original SAM, while also handling video.

### The SA-V dataset

SAM 2 is trained with the same model-in-the-loop philosophy, using an
interactive engine in which annotators correct SAM 2's own masklets frame
by frame. The resulting **SA-V** dataset is the largest video segmentation
resource to date — **50.9K videos** (**196 hours**) with **642.6K masklets**
and **35.5M masks** — deliberately covering whole objects **and their
parts** to match SAM's granularity.

## SAM 3: Segment Anything with Concepts {#sec-sam3}

**SAM 3 (November 2025)** [@carion2025sam3] takes the decisive step from
**geometric** prompting (a point/box/mask always refers to *one* object)
to **conceptual** prompting. It introduces **Promptable Concept
Segmentation (PCS)**: given a **concept prompt** — a **short noun phrase**
(e.g. *"yellow school bus"*, *"striped cat"*), one or more **image
exemplars**, or a combination — the model must **detect, segment, and
track *every* instance** of that concept across an image or video, each
with a unique identity. This aligns SAM with the **open-vocabulary**
goal of modern instance segmentation: exhaustively finding *all*
occurrences of an open-ended category, rather than a single prompted
object. SAM 3 also retains SAM 2's interactive **PVS** capabilities.

![The two tasks SAM 3 supports, in images and video. **Left — Promptable Visual Segmentation (PVS):** positive/negative *points* select a single object (inherited from SAM 2). **Right — Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS):** a *noun phrase* ("a striped cat", "a round cell", "a kangaroo", "hard hat") and/or positive/negative *image exemplars* segment **every** matching instance. *Source: SAM 3, "Segment Anything with Concepts" (2025).*](/images/segmentation/sam3_task.png){#fig-sam3-task width=95%}

**Architecture — a decoupled detector + tracker sharing one backbone.**
SAM 3 is an **848M-parameter** model built from:

- A **shared vision backbone** feeding both sub-systems.
- An **image-level detector** — a **DETR-based** (@sec-detr) model
  conditioned on the concept prompt (text, image exemplars, or geometry),
  which localizes and segments all instances in a frame.
- A **memory-based video tracker** that **inherits the SAM 2** streaming
  memory design (@sec-sam2) to propagate instance identities across
  frames.

A central innovation is the **presence head**, which **decouples
recognition from localization**. Rather than asking each detection query
to simultaneously decide *"is this concept present?"* and *"where is
it?"*, a dedicated **presence token** answers the *what/whether* question
globally, freeing the query embeddings to focus on *where*. This
disentanglement markedly improves discrimination between **similar
concepts** and boosts detection accuracy — particularly with the **hard
negatives** (visually confusable non-matches) baked into training.

![SAM 3 architecture. A **text encoder** and **image encoder** embed the concept prompt ("a penguin"), optional image **exemplar**, and current frame. A **Detector** (new in SAM 3) segments all matching instances in frame $t$, while a **Tracker** (inherited from SAM 2, with its **Memory Bank**) propagates masks from frame $t{-}1$; the two mask sets are merged into the output for frame $t$. Colours mark components from the prompt encoder (PE), from SAM 2, and new in SAM 3. *Source: SAM 3, "Segment Anything with Concepts" (2025).*](/images/segmentation/sam3_model.png){#fig-sam3-model width=95%}

**Data — the SA-Co data engine.** SAM 3 is trained on **Segment Anything
with Concepts (SA-Co)**, produced by a scalable data engine that mixes AI
annotators with humans and yields on the order of **4M unique concept
labels** (including deliberate hard negatives) across images and videos —
far beyond the closed vocabularies of COCO or LVIS.

![The SA-Co data engine. Starting from a **media pool** and an **ontology**, the loop mines data, **proposes noun phrases (NPs)**, and uses **SAM 3** to propose masks; candidates are checked by **AI verifiers** and **human verifiers**. Passing masks become final annotations; failing ("incomplete") masks are **corrected** and fed back, and the accumulated data retrains the model — scaling to millions of concept labels. *Source: SAM 3, "Segment Anything with Concepts" (2025).*](/images/segmentation/sam3_data_engine.png){#fig-sam3-data width=95%}

**Results.** SAM 3 roughly **doubles (≈2×) the accuracy** of prior systems
on both image and video PCS, while **maintaining and improving** SAM 2's
interactive visual-segmentation quality. On the accompanying **SA-Co
benchmark** — which spans **270K unique concepts**, over 50× more than
existing benchmarks — it reaches an estimated **75–80% of human
performance**. Meta open-sourced both the model and the SA-Co benchmark.

**The trajectory in one line.** SAM made segmentation **promptable** and
class-agnostic; SAM 2 made it **temporal**, tracking a prompted object
through video with streaming memory; SAM 3 makes it **conceptual and
exhaustive**, turning a phrase or exemplar into masks for *all* matching
instances across images and video.
